targets.label: GitHub Pages
targets.freeTier: Included with GitHub's plans for public repositories, within GitHub's usage limits; private sites need a paid plan.
targets.cost: Usually no extra charge for a small public site; check the limits on size, bandwidth and builds.
targets.coldStarts: None: the built files are served as they are.
targets.customDomains: Supported, with an HTTPS certificate once DNS points at GitHub.
targets.dataResidency: Served from GitHub's global network; you cannot choose a region.
targets.needs: git, and the GitHub CLI (gh) to open the repository

steps.label: Commit the workflow, then push it
In the repository settings, open Pages and set Source to GitHub Actions
steps.note: The workflow then publishes the site on every push to the branch it watches.

steps.label: Open the repository in your browser

targets.label: Netlify
targets.freeTier: A starter tier for personal projects, with monthly limits on bandwidth, build minutes and function calls.
targets.cost: Paid plans are billed per team member; usage over the limits is billed or paused, depending on the plan.
targets.coldStarts: Static files: none. Functions can take a moment on the first call after they were idle.
targets.customDomains: Supported, with HTTPS certificates Netlify manages.
targets.dataResidency: Static files come from a global network; where functions run depends on the plan.
targets.needs: Node.js (the Netlify CLI runs through npx)

steps.label: Link this folder to a Netlify site
Deploy a draft to check it

targets.label: Render
targets.freeTier: A starter instance type for trying things out; it sleeps when idle and has monthly hour limits.
targets.cost: Always-on instances and databases are billed per month by size.
targets.coldStarts: Starter instances sleep after idle time, so the first request after that is slow.
targets.customDomains: Supported, with HTTPS certificates Render manages.
targets.dataResidency: You pick a region per service (a few regions in the US, Europe and Asia).
targets.needs: git, and a Render account connected to your Git host

steps.label: Push the branch to your Git host
In the Render dashboard, create a Web Service from this repository and choose Docker
steps.note: Set each variable from .env.example in the service settings, never in the repository.

targets.label: Surge
targets.freeTier: A free plan for static sites on a surge.sh address, with limits. Check the provider's current pricing.
targets.cost: A paid plan adds features such as HTTPS on your own domain and password protection.
targets.customDomains: Supported: point the domain at Surge, then publish with the domain instead of the surge.sh name. HTTPS on your own domain needs the paid plan.
targets.dataResidency: Files are served from Surge's own network; there is no region to choose.
targets.needs: Node.js (the Surge CLI runs through npx)

steps.label: Build the site first if it has a build step
steps.note: The command below publishes the folder as it is: the built files, with index.html at its top.

steps.label: Publish the folder to a surge.sh address
steps.note: The first time, the Surge CLI asks for an email and a password in the terminal to make your account. If the name is taken, pick another.

steps.label: For a single-page app, answer every address with the app
steps.note: Copy index.html to 200.html in the same folder before you publish, so links to inner pages load the app.

steps.label: Use your own domain (optional)
steps.note: Point the domain at Surge as its help pages say, then run the publish command with your domain in place of the surge.sh address.

steps.label: Take it down when you no longer want it online

targets.label: Firebase Hosting
targets.freeTier: The Spark plan includes a no-cost allowance of storage and transfer for Hosting. Check the provider's current pricing.
targets.cost: The pay-as-you-go Blaze plan is only needed for some features (such as Cloud Functions); usage past the allowance is billed there.
targets.customDomains: Supported, with HTTPS certificates Firebase provisions.
targets.dataResidency: Static files are served from a global CDN; the Firebase project has a default location.
targets.needs: Node.js and the Firebase CLI (firebase-tools, installed with npm)

steps.label: Sign in to Firebase
steps.note: It opens your browser to sign in. Dim Factory never signs in for you and never keeps the token.

steps.label: Set up Hosting for this folder
steps.note: Pick or create a Firebase project. For the public directory, give the folder with your built files (index.html at its top). For a single-page app, answer Yes to rewriting all URLs to /index.html. Do not let it overwrite your index.html.

steps.label: Check the project id
steps.note: If the Deploy step wrote .firebaserc, replace your-firebase-project-id with your own project id (firebase init does this when you pick a project).

focus: A report about people shows totals, counts and averages: never names, email addresses, phone numbers, street addresses, dates of birth or other personal columns on the page.
Personal columns are left out of every file the page loads (an embedded data copy such as js/data.js, a cleaned CSV): anyone who opens a shared report can read them.
A small group in a breakdown (fewer than five people) can point at one person: merge it into a larger group or leave it out.
The data stays on this computer: no upload to an online service, no analytics or trackers, and no scripts, fonts or pictures from other websites.
Values from the data file are untrusted: they are shown as text (textContent), never as HTML.
